vignette:
At nineteen, he is the youngest person in his lab, the one who still packs his own lunch and whose wedding ring is new enough that he twists it when he thinks. He is a good environmental scientist-meticulous, patient with data, quiet in meetings. His colleagues see a serious young man who speaks four languages and never complains. They do not see what he sees: the way his father's hand still lives inside his chest.

The earliest memory is not a single event but a rhythm. His father came home from his shift at the refinery, and the house grew small. The smell of diesel and sweat. The belt came off first, folded once, then twice. His mother would look at the floor. He learned to stand perfectly still-to make no sound, to become a wall. If he cried, it lasted longer. If he moved, it was unpredictable. So he stopped moving. He stopped making noise. He became very, very still, and that stillness is still inside him.

When he was twelve, his father broke his arm. He told the school he fell off his bike. The doctor believed him, or did not say otherwise. He went home and cleaned the kitchen because his father was asleep and he knew he had to keep the house quiet. That was the year he stopped trying to imagine another life. He started watching documentaries about glaciers, about the way ice holds memory. He decided he would study something that was already frozen, something that could not hurt him.

He left home at seventeen, got married at eighteen to a woman with a soft voice and a family that did not shout. He thought marriage would be a new country, a border he could cross and leave the old one behind. But the old country lives in his body. He wakes up at three in the morning because he hears footsteps that are not there. His wife stirs and asks what's wrong, and he says nothing, because he cannot explain that his father is in the room even though his father is eight hundred miles away.

At work, he is precise. He collects soil samples from contaminated sites, runs them through a mass spectrometer, reads the parts per million of lead, arsenic, cadmium. He likes the numbers because they are honest. He does not like the field work-driving to remote sites, waiting alone in the truck. The waiting is the hardest. When he waits, his mind drifts back. He will find himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles turn white. He will check the rearview mirror three times in thirty seconds. He will not remember deciding to do this.

His wife says he is too jumpy. She says he gets a look in his eyes sometimes, like he is somewhere else. She does not know that when she touches him unexpectedly-a hand on his shoulder-his whole body goes rigid and he tastes copper. He has never told her why he sometimes sleeps on the floor with his back to the wall. He tells himself it's more comfortable that way. He tells himself a lot of things.

The PCL-5 score of 36 means moderate symptoms. He has nightmares about the belt, about the sound of the buckle hitting linoleum. He avoids his family's calls. He cannot stand the sound of a man shouting-even in a movie, even in another language. He startles when his boss walks into his office without knocking. He has a constant low-grade feeling that something bad is about to happen, the way the air feels before a storm. He has learned to function inside this tension. He does his job. He loves his wife. He is still, mostly, a wall.

But sometimes, late at night, he takes out the soil sample reports from the cleanest sites he has ever tested-sites where the contamination is zero, where the earth has been left alone for centuries. He reads the numbers like a prayer. He wants to be a place where nothing toxic was ever buried. He wants to be a place where the ground is safe. He does not know how to get there from here.
